sources.title: Piperno and colleagues, early maize starch and phytoliths from the Central Balsas
sources.note: Direct microfossils on tools and in sediment, maize kernel processing, squash and interpretive tests.

sources.title: Ranere and colleagues, cultural context of early maize and squash in the Central Balsas
sources.note: Shelter stratigraphy, radiocarbon chronology, flaked and ground stone tools, and seasonal cultivators.

sources.title: Smith, reassessing Coxcatlan Cave domesticates
sources.note: Direct AMS dates, stratigraphic movement and the need to test inherited crop chronologies.

sources.title: Piperno and Flannery, earliest archaeological maize from highland Mexico
sources.note: Directly dated Guila Naquitz maize, squash and the long preceramic sequence.

sources.title: Kennett and colleagues, early isotopic evidence for maize as a staple
sources.note: Directly dated human diets, burials, age categories and changing maize reliance in Belize.

sources.title: Nakatsuka and colleagues, south-to-north migration before intensive farming
sources.note: Ancient DNA, population movement, admixture, forest clearance and limits on equating genes with language.

sources.title: Kistler and colleagues, Central American maize genomes and South American gene flow
sources.note: Protracted domestication and later human-mediated movement of maize diversity.

sources.title: Kennett and colleagues, crop chronology at El Gigante rockshelter
sources.note: Hundreds of direct dates on avocado, squash, maize and beans across episodic shelter use.

sources.title: Kistler and colleagues, high-precision maize chronology from El Gigante
sources.note: Direct cob dates, row counts, staple productivity and rockshelter context in Honduras.

sources.title: Perry and colleagues, preceramic maize and root crops in Panama
sources.note: Starch on tools from maize, manioc, yams, arrowroot, Calathea and toxic Zamia.

sources.title: Iizuka and colleagues, manufacture and firing of Monagrillo pottery
sources.note: Clay selection, slab construction, firing temperatures, chronology and seasonal coastal use.

sources.title: Smithsonian, Monagrillo research summary
sources.note: Institutional record for Panama pottery chronology, subsistence and cultural geography.

sources.title: Pratt, function of early San Jacinto pottery
sources.note: Fiber-tempered decorated pottery, mobility and serving or storage interpretations.

sources.title: Oyuela-Caycedo, economic context of early pottery at San Jacinto 1
sources.note: University synthesis of seasonal aggregation, wild plant processing and logistical mobility.

sources.title: Lesure, settlement and subsistence in Early Formative Soconusco
sources.note: Permanent villages from about 1900 BCE, estuary use and vessel-form differences.

sources.title: Clark, Blake and colleagues, origins of privilege in Soconusco
sources.note: Barra and Locona settlements, household inequality, crops and exchange around 1900 to 1500 BCE.

sources.title: Rosenswig and colleagues, settlement in the Cuauhtemoc region of Soconusco
sources.note: Systematic survey evidence for early ceramic villages around 1900 BCE.

sources.title: Museo Nacional de Antropologia, Coxcatlan burial 5
sources.note: Directly dated earlier woman, dental disease, skeletal workload, injury and evidence of care.

sources.title: INAH, Introduction to Puebla archaeology
sources.note: Stone tools, ixtle cord, seeds and cobs preserved in the Tehuacan region.

sources.title: UNESCO, Tehuacan-Cuicatlan Valley World Heritage property
sources.note: Biodiversity, cave evidence, domestication and long-term water-management landscape.

sources.title: UNESCO Man and the Biosphere, Tehuacan-Cuicatlan
sources.note: Environmental diversity, crop history, present Indigenous communities and continuing land use.

sources.title: Kraft and colleagues, multiple lines of evidence for chili domestication
sources.note: Genetics, archaeology, ecology and historical linguistics point to multiregional crop origins.

sources.title: Casas and colleagues, in situ plant management and domestication in Mesoamerica
sources.note: Cultivation, gathering, silviculture and the continuum between wild and domesticated plants.

sources.title: Archaeobotanical evidence for long-term cucurbit use in the Mesoamerican Neotropics
sources.note: Bottle gourds, squash diversity, direct measurement and long-term Indigenous selection.

sources.title: Piperno and Jones, Holocene environmental history of Panama
sources.note: Pollen, phytolith and charcoal evidence for forest interference and horticulture.

sources.title: Aldenderfer and colleagues, four-thousand-year-old gold from Lake Titicaca
sources.note: Secure burial context, cold-hammered gold, pithouses, storage and mixed food production.

sources.title: Rumold and Aldenderfer, potato starch at Jiskairumoko
sources.note: Grinding-tool residues, village features, camelid management and settlement aggregation.

sources.title: Miller and colleagues, Altiplano agricultural origins and resilience
sources.note: Quinoa, tubers, animals, human diets, burials and mixed subsistence in the Titicaca Basin.

sources.title: Stanish and colleagues, obsidian exchange and watercraft in Lake Titicaca
sources.note: Nonlocal obsidian and evidence for lake transport by about 1600 BCE.

sources.title: Holocene Lake Titicaca levels and sociopolitical development
sources.note: Climate, water levels and cautions about connecting environmental change to social change.

sources.title: INAH, San Lorenzo Tenochtitlan archaeological zone
sources.note: Site chronology begins at the atlas endpoint and records later growth, transport and earthwork.

sources.title: INAH, theobromine in San Lorenzo pottery
sources.note: Localized cacao residues in vessels dated across 1800 to 1000 BCE.

sources.title: Cobean and colleagues, early Olmec obsidian trade at San Lorenzo
sources.note: Geochemical sourcing of securely dated obsidian artifacts and exchange-network limits.

sources.title: INAH, the carved Cascajal block
sources.note: A much later possible writing system around 900 BCE, outside the target interval.

sources.title: World Health Organization, natural toxins in food
sources.note: Modern science of cyanogenic glycosides and cassava food safety.

sources.title: EFSA, cyanogenic glycosides and processing
sources.note: Experimental evidence for crushing, soaking, fermenting and roasting to reduce cassava cyanide.

sources.title: Mycotoxins during nixtamalization and tortilla production
sources.note: Modern food science explaining alkaline cooking, steeping and nutritional effects.

sources.title: Santini and colleagues, archaeological evidence for nixtamalization at La Corona
sources.note: Direct vessel evidence is much later, illustrating why exact-period claims require caution.

sources.title: Harrison-Buck and colleagues, Late Archaic fisheries in Belize wetlands
sources.note: Canals, holding ponds, barbed points and evidence for aquatic food strategies around the target era.

sources.title: Arnold and colleagues, ceramic learning in Huancito
sources.note: Later ethnoarchaeological comparison for childhood observation, practice and household apprenticeship.

sources.title: Reinhard and colleagues, food, parasites and epidemiological transitions
sources.note: Archaeoparasitology methods, coprolite limits and broad health comparisons.

sources.title: FAO, maize diversity and farmers practices in Chiapas
sources.note: Present seed selection and exchange, used only as a labeled continuity comparison.

sources.title: Cambridge World Prehistory, Archaic and Formative periods of Mesoamerica
sources.note: Scholarly warning that period boundaries depend on changing archaeological criteria.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Atlas umbrella across parts of Mexico, Central America, Colombia and the Andes, circa 2000 to 1500 BCE.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact indexed id and accented display name are preserved; the id is a historical-basemap key, not a self-name.
One exact Polygon snapshot covers the sole interval from 2000 to 1500 BCE.
The geometry extends far beyond Mesoamerica into Colombia, Cuzco and the Lake Titicaca region while excluding several nearby coasts.
The target is not one people, language, state, ancestry, archaeological culture or uniform economy.
Named sites are localized case studies and are never generalized across the whole polygon.
Direct finds, scientific inference and later ethnographic or food-science comparison are labeled separately.
The 1500 BCE endpoint is an atlas redraw into other editorial categories, not a shared collapse or conquest.
No contemporaneous writing sample is supplied because no secure deciphered script belongs to this exact category and interval.
Predecessor and successor arrays remain empty because the atlas umbrella is not a historical polity or ethnicity.
